extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and litigants in U.S. patent litigation (equity practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules governing equitable ancillary proceedings (bills of revivor, discovery, perpetuation of testimony) and the grant/refusal of preliminary and perpetual injunctions in patent infringement litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of Revivor — grounds and who may file
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for leave to file a supplemental bill in the nature of a bill of review must show that the petitioner could not with reasonable diligence have discovered the alleged new matters before the hearing and decision, and that the new matter is material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bill of revivor will not be granted when the petitioner could, by diligent attention to the exhibits attached to the original bill, have found out what he now relies on, or where the decree will be the same. A bill of revivor is not to be filed by the assignee of the original complainant but only by the legal representatives of a deceased party; revivor lies only where the cause of action would survive. An administrator’s filing after interlocutory decree does not revive the case unless the court so orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill to Perpetuate Testimony — when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill to perpetuate testimony is required whenever it becomes apparent that on a future action (which the proper plaintiff refuses to commence or cannot yet begin) certain evidence will be important and though now available may later be beyond the petitioner's reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If allegations are sustained by proof, the court will have the testimony taken in a suitable manner and preserved among the records until needed at trial. A bill to perpetuate testimony will not be granted where a suit can at once be brought by the petitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill of Discovery — purpose and prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: A bill of discovery prays for the compulsory disclosure of certain facts within the respondent’s knowledge and is ordinarily employed only in aid of suits at law or as collateral/introductory to other equitable proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill must aver some right in the petitioner which the discovery might help to vindicate, and demand information which might constitute a ground for some claim or defense in the principal action. The respondent must be a party to such action (not simply a witness). Under a mere bill of discovery the petitioner obtains no other assistance than the disclosure asked; but if the bill contains a prayer for general relief the court may grant such relief as the facts disclosed require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery in patent cases is akin to inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery in patent cases is of the nature of an inspection and is more effective than adverse testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity can compel inspection and discovery in ways a court of law cannot; a bill of discovery will lie in the Circuit Court as ancillary to a suit for infringement irrespective of citizenship. Discovery is often treated as inspection rather than mere testimonial disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be compelled to answer — corporations and oath
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation may be called upon for a discovery and must answer; but if a disclosure under oath is to be ordered, its officers must also be made parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a discovery is to be on oath, officers of a corporate respondent must be made parties so that the court may require sworn answers. If discovery is imperfectly pleaded, the bill cannot be treated as one for general relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on discovery (royalties, plaintiff title, cross-bills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain forms of discovery are limited: a bill of discovery of royalties due is not allowable except in aid of an action at law; a defendant cannot demand discovery from the plaintiff as to his title and its source and validity by a cross-bill unless he alleges title in himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery of royalties or other matters inappropriate to pure discovery will be disallowed unless ancillary to a legal action. A defendant must plead an interest (title) in himself before he can use discovery to contest the plaintiff’s title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and proper use of injunctive relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The exercise of preventive jurisdiction by equity (injunctions) is the most potent method for protecting the owner of a patent: it removes danger of irremediable injury, prevents multiplicity of suits, and enforces the patent monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An injunction is the strong arm of the court, prompt and effective, and should be applied unhesitatingly where the plaintiff cannot otherwise escape irreparable or repeated injuries—but never when other remedies are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of injunctions — preliminary vs. perpetual
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions in infringement actions may be preliminary or perpetual. A preliminary injunction issues at the commencement or during pendency to preserve the status quo while investigation proceeds. A perpetual injunction is a decree upon the merits permanently prohibiting infringing acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary injunctions are temporary measures to preserve affairs while the court determines rights; perpetual injunctions follow full merits adjudication and end the defendant’s manufacture/use/sale of the invention until patent expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions are discretionary and fact-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction is not a matter of course and cannot be governed by any fixed rules; its allowance or refusal depends on innumerable qualifying circumstances and rests entirely with the discretion of the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While broad discretion is allowed, it must be exercised in conformity with equity practice and precedents. The judge should determine each case by reference to equity principles and analogous precedents; discretion is not arbitrary but guided by established equitable principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and limits of preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction is intended to prevent prospective injury and must be confined to that purpose; it cannot be used for punishment of past infringements, coercion, or to restrain third parties from contracting with an alleged infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is an auxiliary remedy applied only where the right is probable and the invasion apparent; where the right is doubtful, the wrong uncertain, or other temporary protection equally beneficial and less injurious exists, the injunction should be refused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions generally non-appealable
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue or refusal of a preliminary injunction rests in the court’s discretion, and from its judgment there is no appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because circumstances vary and judicial judgment differs, the law concedes wide liberty to courts in this exercise of discretion; appellate correction of preliminary rulings is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors courts weigh in deciding injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding a motion for injunction courts consider the condition of the litigation, the nature of the invention, the character and extent of the infringement, and the effect of the injunction on interests of plaintiff and defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These considerations must motivate the court’s decision; analogy of precedents and established equity rules are the controlling guide while the judge weighs the evidence and justice between antagonistic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three essential prerequisites for preliminary injunction in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary injunction will be granted only when the court is satisfied: (1) that the patent is valid; (2) that the plaintiff is the owner of a legal or equitable interest therein; and (3) that the defendant is about to commit an act of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reasonable doubt exists as to any one of these points the injunction will be denied; even when they are established other circumstances may render its allowance inexpedient or inequitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to prove patent validity for preliminary relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity of the patent must be proved either by the judgment of some competent tribunal, by the long-continued acquiescence of the public in the exclusive privilege, or by some other act or fact equivalent thereto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent by itself is prima facie evidence but insufficient alone for preliminary injunctive relief; exclusive possession/use for a sufficient period, public acquiescence, or a prior judgment sustaining the patent are the principal acceptable proofs. Admissions by the defendant may supplement where judgments and acquiescence are lacking. Courts often require these definite, easily procured forms of proof in preliminary hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts will not anticipate final merits by extended examination
rubrics_metrics.description: On a motion for a preliminary injunction the court will not anticipate the trial on the merits by an extended examination of testimony; in obscure propositions or disputed intricate facts the court will refuse the injunction until these matters are investigated in their proper order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This attitude has led to peculiar rules of evidence for preliminary hearings: plaintiffs are required to furnish certain special forms of proof, or else await the final hearing before invoking preventive power. The court will examine just enough to see whether equitable rights require protection during litigation.
